##### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.14.3.10 — `credential_binding_ref` selects a credential, and nothing authorizes the selection

- Opened: `pending` by `.11.14.3.4`, which measured it while binding the read and deliberately did not fold two decisions into one slice.
- 🔴 **The field is caller-supplied and it is a SELECTOR.** `ResourceReference.credential_binding_ref` arrives on `POST /v1/resources` as free text, and `api.rs`'s R5 arm reads it back out of the stored row and hands it to `broker.resolve(&binding)`. `crates/reasonbraid-server/src/broker.rs`'s store is `HashMap<String, Credential>` — **no tenant, anywhere** — so the binding namespace is global and a binding name is the whole predicate for reaching a credential. ⛔ ROADMAP §16.3 invariant 5: *"target credentials are selected only after authorization for the concrete target and action."*
- ⭐ **And the pair key makes it shared.** `UNIQUE (original_locator, expected_digest)` means a second tenant registering the same pair inherits the FIRST tenant's `credential_binding_ref` — its own value is discarded by the replay. Two tenants citing one URL cannot hold two different bindings, which is a consequence of `.11.14.3.2`'s key that nobody had stated.
- ⚠️ **THE WIDTH IS MEASURED AND IT IS LATENT, NOT LIVE.** `grep -rn "\.register(" crates/ --include=*.rs | grep -i broker` returns **3** hits and **all three are tests** — two in `broker.rs`'s own `#[cfg(test)]` module, one in `profiles.rs`. `grep -rn "Broker" crates/reasonbraid-server/src/bin/*.rs` returns **0**: `rb-server` reaches `Broker::default()` through `ApiState::new`, an empty store. And `RB_ENABLE_R5R3RX` is off by default. So every shipped deployment answers `credential_unavailable` and there is no credential to reach. ⛔ Publishing this as a live cross-tenant credential path would have been a claim derived by READING — this tree's repeated failure mode — and it is recorded at its real width instead.
- ⭐ **It is `.13.1.1`'s shape**: a finished mechanism with no production producer, which is exactly the state in which a design defect is cheapest to fix and least likely to be noticed. The day a deployment registers a binding, it is live.
- Owns: deciding what authorizes a credential selection — whether a binding is tenant-scoped in the broker, whether the reference may name one at all, or whether the selection moves off the shared row entirely; and stating what the pair key implies for a field two tenants cannot hold separately.
- ⛔ Do NOT assume the answer is a tenant column on the broker. The broker's deployment integration is named as the OS keychain, out of the dev profile's scope, so a dev-store change may not be the durable one. And a reference that cannot name a binding needs somewhere else for the selection to live — §12.1 lists the field.
- Acceptance: the selection is reproduced by command with the gate on and a registered binding (a second tenant reaching a binding it did not name), RED first; the disposition is recorded with its rejected alternatives; the pair-key consequence is stated in the book beside the limits already published there; and the existing R5 controls pass.
- 🔴 **REPRODUCED, RED FIRST, and the measurement is the leaf's centre.** Gate open (`start_gated`), ONE binding registered with the broker, two enrolled tenants, one locator. The stranger replayed the pair naming **no** binding and its resolve answered `resolvers: ["r5-credential-broker"]` → `destination_refused` — and `destination_refused` is the **loopback pre-flight**, which is reached only once a credential has RESOLVED. The stranger drove an authenticated acquisition with the owner's credential.
- ⭐ **The discriminator is the RESOLVER, not the error kind**, and naming it was the difference between a control that proves something and one that passes. Both the authenticated and the unauthenticated path end at the same loopback `destination_refused`; only `resolvers` says which one ran. ⛔ The first draft of arm 2 asserted `credential_unavailable` and would have FAILED against the repaired product — because the repair reaches one layer further than denying the credential (below).
- ⭐ **DECIDED: the selector moves off the shared row onto `reference_registrations`, and `migrations/0069` DROPS the old column.** The shared row keeps the CONTENT; the tenant-bound row keeps the DECISION. That is this family's own correction for the fourth time — citations, assessments, reference reads, and now a means of ACCESS, which is the sharpest of the four.
- ⭐ **The repair is wider than a denial, which the reproduction only revealed once it was run.** `resolvers::resolve` takes the binding as a RANKING input: a binding ranks only the `credential`-class packs, a binding-less reference only the `none`-class ones. So a tenant that named no binding is **not routed to the credential broker at all** — it gets R0. That is a stronger property than "the credential is refused" and it was measured, not designed.
- ⭐ **And the pair-key limit closes in the OTHER direction, which nobody had stated.** `UNIQUE (original_locator, expected_digest)` meant two tenants citing one URL could not hold two DIFFERENT bindings — the second's value was discarded by the replay. Both may now. The sharing had only ever been discussed as a leak, never as a limit.
- ⭐ **The strongest part of the fix is structural.** `resources::get` (the private UNBOUND read) now has no column to read a selector from, so it returns `None` unconditionally: an unbound read of a shared row CANNOT yield a credential selector — not by convention, by schema.
- ⛔ **Four alternatives rejected, and the ⛔ this leaf opened with was the first of them.** A tenant column on the BROKER (its deployment integration is the OS keychain — a machine-local operator store with no tenant dimension; the dev `HashMap` would be the only place the change was real); taking the binding on the RESOLVE REQUEST instead (more caller-supplied, not less); keeping it on the shared row and honouring it only for its writer (leaves the pair-key limit AND a live selector on a shared row); and keeping the dropped column unread (a dead credential selector is the next author's mistake, already in the schema — `.11.14.3.5` had to repair a dead column that only held a risk class).
- ⚠️ **The backfill is EXACT, and that is the only reason a credential may be moved at all.** `reference_registrations.registered_by` and `resource_references.submitted_by` are literally the same value — `api::submit_resource` writes `actor_handle_for_subject` into one and clones it into the other — so the submitter joins precisely to its own registration and every other tenant's gets `NULL`. §16.4: *secret access fails closed.* ⛔ Had no such join existed, the honest backfill would have been NOBODY.
- ⚠️ **`DO NOTHING` on the audit columns, `DO UPDATE` on the binding, and the asymmetry is deliberate.** `registered_at`/`registered_by` are history and a re-registration must not rewrite them; the binding is this tenant's CURRENT access decision, and a submission is the complete statement of a reference (`.11.14.3.5`'s settled rule), so re-submitting without one clears it. Any other rule makes a credential selector impossible to withdraw.
- 🔴 **A defect of my own, found by the neighbours rather than by my control.** The new control opened the opt-in gate and left it open; `resolver_capabilities` is migration-seeded and deliberately absent from this suite's cleanup plan, so `the_gated_packs_resolve_only_while_the_gate_is_open` failed on its CLOSED phase. ⛔ Closing the gate at the END of my test was NOT the fix — a test that PANICS never reaches its own end, which is exactly how it was found, since my control was RED at the time. The gate is now normalised in `pool()` beside the other fixtures, so the starting state does not depend on how the previous test finished.
- **FALSIFIED.** Source and `migrations/0069` stashed together (the source alone would read a dropped column and error rather than regress), control left in place, stash **verified to have landed** — `git status` showing only the control dirty and `0069` absent — then the suite went RED at exactly the defect arm: `Array [String("r5-credential-broker")]` where the repair gives `Array [String("r0-https-fetcher")]`. Restored and re-verified.
- **No regression:** `profiles` 55/55 (the suite that owns every `/v1/resources` control — a census shows it is the only one that exercises the route), `migration_upgrade` 4/4 and `backup_restore` 1/1 (the two suites a `DROP COLUMN` would break), `reasonbraid-server --lib` 113/113, clippy `-D warnings` clean.
- Routed OUT: the broker's namespace is still global — a tenant may NAME a binding an operator created for another tenant. `.11.14.3.10.1` owns it.
- Decision: `docs/decisions/2026-09-17_a-credential-binding-is-tenant-bound.md`. Promoted: `docs/knowledge/a-shared-row-may-not-hold-a-tenant-decision.md`.
- lockstep: README.md unchanged (objective, layout and standard commands untouched; this leaf moves one column and publishes the disposition in the book chapter that already documented the limit).
- Status: `done`.
- Verification / commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0234`.

###### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.14.3.10.1 — The broker's binding namespace is global, so naming a binding is still the whole predicate

- Opened: `pending` by `.11.14.3.10`, which closed the INHERITANCE half and measured that the naming half is a different mechanism.
- 🔴 **The remaining defect, stated exactly.** A tenant may write any binding name into its OWN registration and reach the credential an operator registered for someone else. `.11.14.3.10` removed the silent inheritance — the name now has to be typed — but typing it is still sufficient, and ROADMAP §16.3 invariant 5 wants an authorization BEFORE the selection: *"target credentials are selected only after authorization for the concrete target and action."*
- ⛔ **Why it is not a wiring change, which is why it is not folded into its parent.** `crates/reasonbraid-server/src/authority.rs` has the machinery — boundaries, scoped grants, `authorize` writing an audit row for allowances AND denials — but its vocabulary does not reach here: `GrantAction` is `thread_*` plus `TenantAdmin` (**10 variants, 0 about a resource or a credential**) and `TargetSelector` is thread/tenant-shaped. Authorizing a credential selection means a NEW action and a NEW selector, which is a §16.4 authorization surface, not a call site.
- ⛔ **And `.11.6` bars proposing the rule before its population is measured.** `grep -rn "\.register(" crates/ --include=*.rs | grep -i broker` returns **3** hits and **all three are tests**; `grep -rn "Broker" crates/reasonbraid-server/src/bin/*.rs` returns **0**. The population of operator-granted bindings is ZERO, so there is nothing yet to shape a grant vocabulary against.
- ⚠️ **LATENT, not live**, on that same census — the R5 pack is off by default (`RB_ENABLE_R5R3RX`) and every shipped deployment runs an empty broker store. ⭐ `.13.1.1`'s shape again: a finished mechanism with no production producer, which is when a design defect is cheapest to fix and least likely to be noticed.
- Owns: deciding what authorizes a credential selection once the authority engine has a vocabulary that can express one — the action, the selector, the fail-closed rule when no grant matches, and whether the operator's grant is per binding or per credential class.
- Acceptance: the naming reach is reproduced by command (a tenant registering a binding an operator created for another tenant) before it is decided; the decision names its rejected alternatives; the refusal is typed and recorded like every other authorization decision; and the published limit in `docs/book/src/deployment.md` is rewritten by the leaf that closes it.
- Verification / commit: pending.

##### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.14.3.5 — `POST /v1/resources` takes §12.1 fields nothing validates, and its omissions bypass the column defaults

- Opened: `pending` by `.11.14.3.2`, which derived the citation path's `scheme` from the locator and thereby measured what the route does instead.
- 🔴 **`scheme` is a caller-supplied field validated against nothing.** `crates/reasonbraid-server/tests/profiles.rs`'s own helper says so in a comment — *"`resource_references.scheme` is caller-supplied and is NOT validated against the locator, so a control that wrote `https` here would be routed on data that is simply false"* — and §12.2 ranks resolvers on the scheme. A reference claiming `https` for a `ftp://` locator is routed on a lie. ⭐ `.11.14.3.2`'s `resources::scheme_of` is the check and is already written; what is undecided is whether applying it to the route is a compatibility break worth taking.
- 🔴 **The `NOT NULL DEFAULT` clauses on `visibility_scope` and `risk_class` are dead.** `migrations/0023` declares `DEFAULT 'network'` and `DEFAULT 'low'`; `ResourceReference` declares `#[serde(default)]` on both, which is `String::default()` — the empty string — and `resources::submit` binds it explicitly, so the column default never applies. Every reference the shipped controls submit without those fields holds `''`, and `''` is not a risk class. ⚠️ Inert TODAY, and the census says so rather than the sentence — pinned at `69b6374`, the commit before `.11.14.3.2`: `git grep -c 'risk_class\|visibility_scope' 69b6374 -- crates/reasonbraid-server/src` returns **14 hits outside `policy.rs`** (which owns an unrelated `risk_class` on a policy version) — **10** in `resources.rs`'s own struct, SQL and row mapping, and **4** in `fetcher.rs`/`snapshots.rs`, two apiece, building a THROWAWAY `ResourceReference` only to reuse `digest_error()`. **Zero read the stored column for a decision**, which is why `.11.14.3.2` did not widen to it — but §12.2 says resolution "first applies authorization and risk filters", so it stops being inert the moment that filter is built.
- ⚠️ **A third field, found while building the citation path and left alone deliberately: `fragment_or_selector`.** §12.1 lists it beside `original_locator`, which implies the locator excludes the fragment — but both writers store the locator VERBATIM, so `…/page#a` and `…/page#b` are two references over identical bytes and `…/page` is a third. ⛔ `.11.14.3.2` declined to split it out, because splitting IS canonicalization and §12.1 says canonicalization "must not erase security-relevant distinctions" — merging three locators onto one row is exactly such an erasure, and deciding it needs the scheme-specific rules §12.1 defers. ⭐ The conservative choice costs a shared row; the other choice costs a distinction, which is the harder one to get back.
- ⚠️ **The citation path already diverges, deliberately and recorded.** `.11.14.3.2` writes the schema's declared defaults because a contributor states neither field. So one column currently holds `''` from one writer and `'low'` from the other — a divergence this leaf closes in whichever direction it decides.
- Owns: deciding whether the route validates `scheme` against its locator; deciding what an omitted `visibility_scope`/`risk_class` means and making both writers agree; deciding whether a locator's fragment belongs in `original_locator` or in `fragment_or_selector`; and the compatibility disposition for each.
- Acceptance: each of the THREE — the unvalidated `scheme`, the dead column defaults, the in-locator fragment — is reproduced by command before it is decided; each decision names its rejected alternatives; after it a reference's scheme either matches its locator or is refused by name; the two writers produce the same row for the same omitted field; the fragment's disposition is stated even if it is "leave it"; and the existing reference controls pass.
- **THREE mechanisms, THREE arms, and they are separated on purpose** — deciding three from two reproductions is the over-reporting `.11.15` exists to catch. All three ride one control, `a_reference_s_declared_fields_are_checked_or_defaulted`.
- 🔴 **(1) REFUTED, AND THE ROUTE TO THE REFUTATION IS THE LEAF'S MAIN DELIVERABLE.** The premise came from a test helper's comment — *"`resource_references.scheme` is caller-supplied and is NOT validated against the locator, so a control that wrote `https` here would be routed on data that is simply false"* — beside the facts that §12.2 ranks resolvers on the field and that `resources::scheme_of` exists with one caller. ⛔ **I wrote the check, reproduced RED against it (`ftp://example.org/archive.tar` declared `https` registered, `200`), went GREEN on my own control — and two of this suite's OWN controls then refused it**: `the_r1_resolver_resolves_git_…` and `the_gated_packs_resolve_only_while_the_gate_is_open`.
- ⭐ **Measured instead of inferred.** The consumer is one predicate — `resolvers::resolve`'s `WHERE schemes @> $1::jsonb` over `resolver_capabilities` — and **two SHIPPED packs pair a non-URI scheme with an `https://*` locator pattern**: `r1-git-fetcher` advertises `["git"]` (`migrations/0026`) and the R3 browser pack advertises `["web+render"]` (`resolvers.rs`). A Git repository and a rendered page are both reached over HTTPS. **The field is how a caller asks for a CAPABILITY**, and was never a claim about the locator.
- ⭐ **(1) DECIDED: no check; the contract is STATED.** The meaning is recorded at the type and in the book, a control arm pins the refutation (`git` and `web+render` register for `https://` locators), and the helper comment that produced the wrong premise is corrected **at its source** — a sentence that produced one wrong repair will produce another. ⚠️ The field is validated against nothing else either, deliberately: §3.7 says accepting a reference is not a promise the core can resolve it, so an unadvertised scheme is `resource_unresolvable_now` at RESOLUTION, and a second arm pins that. ⛔ A shape check on the token was considered and rejected under `.11.6` — a rule may not be proposed before its population is measured, and no census of malformed scheme tokens exists; inventing one is how this section went wrong the first time.
- 🔎 **What caught it, recorded because it is the transferable part:** the two refusing controls are not about references — they exercise the PACKS, and the packs are the consumer. **A repair is falsified by the code that USES the thing, which is the same place its contract lives.** Running the affected suites BROADLY rather than only this leaf's own control is what surfaced it; the narrow run was green. Promoted as `docs/knowledge/a-fields-name-is-not-its-contract.md`.
- 🔴 **(2) REPRODUCE + the shape of the defect.** `migrations/0023` declares `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'network'` and `DEFAULT 'low'`; `#[serde(default)]` is `String::default()` — the EMPTY STRING — and `submit` binds the field explicitly, so the column default never applied. The citation path writes the declared values, so **the two writers produced different rows for the same omission**. The control asserts the repaired state by COMPARING the two writers' rows rather than by asserting a literal twice.
- ⭐ **(2) DECIDED: the serde default IS the schema's declared default.** ⚠️ That is the permissive direction and it is ADOPTED rather than chosen — `low` is what the migration already recorded and the citation path already writes. ⛔ §12.2's risk filter does not exist (no site reads either column for a decision), and when it is built it owns whether `low` may be a default at all. Stated at the field, not only here.
- ⭐ **(3) DECIDED: the fragment stays in the locator, and the arm pins the behaviour rather than a repair.** Three spellings are three references. ⛔ Splitting IS canonicalization, which §12.1 defers as scheme-specific and which would erase a distinction that section protects. ⭐ **This is the same boundary `.11.14.3.13` drew from the other side** — a STRICT comparison normalises nothing and is not a canonicalization decision, while SPLITTING a locator is one — so the two leaves agree and the line between them is stated rather than felt.
- ⚠️ **Left alone deliberately:** the throwaway `ResourceReference` values in `fetcher.rs` and `snapshots.rs` carry `"tenant"`/`"standard"`, matching neither writer. They exist only to reuse `digest_error()` and are never stored; harmonising them would imply they mean something.
- ⚠️ **So the leaf closes with ONE repair and TWO stated contracts, not three repairs.** That is the honest count: the goal line named three mechanisms, one was a real defect, one was a design the leaf had misread, and one was already decided the conservative way. ⭐ `.11.6`'s rule — measure the population before proposing the rule — is what a raw "three findings, three fixes" reading would have violated.
- Decision: `docs/decisions/2026-09-17_a-reference-s-declared-fields-are-checked-or-defaulted.md`.
- lockstep: README.md unchanged (objective, layout and standard commands untouched; this leaf checks two request fields and publishes all three dispositions in the book chapter that documents the reference contract).
- Status: `done`.
- Verification / commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0228`.

##### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.14.3.6 — The `expected_digest` pin is recorded and never enforced

- Opened: `pending` by `.11.14.3.2`, which made the pin the reference's IDENTITY and therefore made "what does the pin do" a question with an answer.
- 🔴 **Nothing checks an acquired snapshot's bytes against its reference's pin — the census, classified rather than counted.**

Pinned at `69b6374`, the commit before `.11.14.3.2` — which adds four hits of its own, so the working tree measures the repair rather than the defect:

```bash
git grep -n expected_digest 69b6374 -- crates/reasonbraid-server/src   # -> 13 hits in 3 files
```

  Ten are `resources.rs`'s own store (the struct field, the ADR-011 validator, the three SQL statements, the row mapping); `fetcher.rs:1257` and `snapshots.rs:89` each build a THROWAWAY `ResourceReference` **only to reuse `digest_error()`**, never reading a stored row; `snapshots.rs:71` is a doc comment about the uniqueness constraint. **Zero read a STORED pin**, and `.11.14.3.2`'s four additions are the registration path writing one, not reading one. `snapshots::submit` verifies that the bytes hash to the *submission's own* `raw_digest` (content-addressing verified, not trusted) and that the `reference_id` exists — and then never reads `resource_references.expected_digest`. So a reference pinned to `sha256:aaa…` accepts a snapshot of entirely different bytes, and the §12.1 field a caller supplied to say "these are the bytes I expect" constrains nothing.
- ⭐ **This is older than `.11.14.3.2` and was invisible because of it.** While `resources::submit` refused a second digest per locator, the pin looked like an immutability rule and read as though it were enforced somewhere. With the pair as the key, the pin is plainly a declared expectation with no checkpoint.
- ⚠️ **Not obviously a defect, and the leaf must decide rather than assume.** `evidence_snapshots` replays on `(reference_id, raw_digest)`, so one reference is already designed to hold many versions; a pin enforced at acquisition would forbid exactly that. The honest candidates are: enforce at acquisition (and forbid the plural), record a MISMATCH on the snapshot (and let the reader see it), or state that the pin is a caller's note and say so where §12.1 is documented.
- Owns: measuring what reads `expected_digest` today; deciding the pin's meaning; and publishing it wherever the reference contract is described.
- Acceptance: a control observes a snapshot accepted against a reference pinned to different bytes, RED first if the disposition is enforcement; the disposition is recorded with its rejected alternatives; and the book states what a pin does rather than leaving a reader to infer it from the field's name.
- **RE-DERIVED on the working tree, not quoted from the pin above.** `git grep -n expected_digest -- crates/reasonbraid-server/src` now returns **20** hits rather than the 13 recorded at `69b6374`; the growth is `.11.14.3.2`'s registration path and `.11.14.3.4`'s registration set writing the column, not reading it. The classification is unchanged: `snapshots::submit` asked `SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM resource_references WHERE resource_id = $1)` and **zero** sites read a STORED pin.
- 🔴 **REPRODUCE, falsified against the exact unrepaired store** — the production file reverted with `git stash push -- crates/reasonbraid-server/src/snapshots.rs`, the control run, the file restored. A reference pinned to `sha256(the audited figure is 41.2 per cent)` accepted a snapshot of `the audited figure is 62.8 per cent`: `200 {"replay":false,"snapshot_id":"snp_01a0aec59be97d93af711df98b146e90"}`, `46 passed; 1 failed`.
- ⭐ **DECIDED: a pinned reference accepts only the bytes it names; an unpinned one is unchanged** (`docs/decisions/2026-09-17_a-pin-names-its-bytes.md`, three alternatives rejected). The leaf's own framing — *"a pin enforced at acquisition would forbid exactly that [plural]"* — resolves rather than binds: the plural belongs to the UNPINNED reference, and `evidence_snapshots`'s `(reference_id, raw_digest)` replay keeps it there. ⭐ **Enforcement is what makes `.11.14.3.2`'s pair key mean something**: that leaf made `(locator, digest)` the identity so a changed page would be a SECOND reference, and with no checkpoint both rows accepted any bytes, so the distinction the key was created to preserve was preserved nowhere.
- **FIX** — the lookup returns `expected_digest` instead of asking `EXISTS`: the outer `Option` is existence, the inner one is the pin. `SnapshotError::PinMismatch` refuses before anything is written, and ⛔ **carries NEITHER digest** — the caller holds the actual one and the pinned one belongs to a reference this route does not check the caller may read, so quoting it would be an oracle over a `res_…` id. The message carries the next step instead, which is the part a legitimate caller does not already have. In the STORE rather than at the resolver, for `.11.14.3.8`'s reason: four call sites reach it and a fifth would inherit the hole.
- **ADDRESSED (verified)** — the pinned reference refuses other bytes `400` with the pin named as the reason, quotes neither digest, and writes **0** rows; it accepts its own bytes; an **unpinned** reference still holds **2** versions; and the same locator at the other digest is a second reference that acquires normally. `RB_DEMO=0 bash scripts/run_pg_tests.sh profiles` → **47 passed / 0 failed**.
- ⛔ **CONSEQUENCE, stated rather than discovered.** `api.rs`'s R0 and R5 arms call `let _ = crate::snapshots::submit(…)`, so a pinned reference whose page drifted now returns an acquisition receipt and no snapshot, SILENTLY. The discard predates this leaf — its own comment says *"a persistence failure leaves the receipt returned"* — and what changed is that it now has a likely, caller-meaningful cause. Censused: `grep -n "crate::snapshots::submit" crates/reasonbraid-server/src/*.rs` returns **4** sites and the R2 arm already captures its result, so it is **two**. Owned by `.11.14.3.12`.
- ROUTING EVIDENCE: `.11.14.3.11` and `.11.14.3.12` are both opened from this leaf's execution. ⭐ `.11.14.3.11` is a gap in **my own census one commit earlier**: `.11.14.3.4` enumerated the routes under `/v1/resources` and bound them, and `POST /v1/snapshots` names a reference in its BODY — the same blind spot `.3.5.3` recorded, in a different family. What was measured is that the route is enrolment-gated and distinguishes `ReferenceMissing` from every other answer, so it is an existence oracle over `res_…` ids of exactly the class `.11.14.3.4` closed. `.11.14.3.12` reproduces only with a pinned reference and a drifted page; the discard itself is older than both leaves.
- lockstep: README.md unchanged (objective, layout and standard commands untouched; this leaf enforces one stored field and publishes it in the book chapter that documents the reference contract).
- Status: `done`.
- Verification / commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0224`.

##### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.14.3.11 — `POST /v1/snapshots` names a reference it never checks the caller may use

- Opened: `pending` by `.11.14.3.6`, and it is a gap in `.11.14.3.4`'s own census one commit earlier rather than a new surface.
- 🔴 **The census that missed it, and why.** `.11.14.3.4` enumerated the routes under `/v1/resources` — `grep -n '"/v1/resources' crates/reasonbraid-server/src/api.rs` → 3 — and bound the two that read a reference. `POST /v1/snapshots` names a `reference_id` in its **BODY**, so a route-prefix census cannot see it. ⭐ That is `.3.5.3`'s shape exactly (*a census correct about its own scope and silent about what fell outside it*), in a different family and committed by the same session that had just written the rule down.
- **The finding.** `submit_snapshot` admits on enrolment alone and passes the caller's `reference_id` straight to the store, which answers `ReferenceMissing` for an absent id and proceeds for any other. So a caller holding a `res_…` id it never registered can distinguish existence — and, on success, attach a snapshot to another tenant's reference and cite it.
- ⚠️ **Weaker than it sounds, and the leaf must not inflate it.** `resource_id` is `res_<uuid>` and unguessable, there is no list verb, and since `.11.14.3.4` the detail read and the resolve verb are already bound — so the id is reachable only through the pair replay, which registers the caller anyway. The question is whether a WRITE against a reference should require what the READ requires.
- Owns: reproducing the oracle by command (a second tenant distinguishing an absent `reference_id` from a foreign one); deciding whether the snapshot write takes the same registration binding the read took; and stating what it means for a snapshot to be attached to a reference by a tenant that did not register it.
- ⛔ Do NOT assume symmetry with the read settles it. A snapshot submission carries the BYTES, so a caller reaching this route already holds the content — which is the asymmetry that made the snapshot family's replay safe in `.11.14.3.4`'s own reasoning, and it cuts the other way here.
- Acceptance: the oracle is reproduced RED first if the disposition is a binding; the disposition is recorded with its rejected alternatives; and `.11.14.3.4`'s record gains the correction or the explicit confirmation that its census stands for the routes it enumerated.
- 🔴 **REPRODUCE, RED first, and it is a WRITE as well as an oracle.** The stranger's submission against the owner's reference and against an absent id, side by side:

```text
foreign: 200 {"replay":false,"snapshot_id":"snp_01a0aee3660d7d32906d5524d6423f98"}
absent:  400 {"code":"invalid_command","message":"the reference does not exist"}
```

  `48 passed; 1 failed`. So it was not only distinguishable — the foreign submission **succeeded**, attaching a snapshot to a reference another tenant registered.
- **The census that measured the consequence.** `grep -rn "WHERE reference_id" crates/reasonbraid-server/src/*.rs` returns **1** — the replay lookup inside `submit` itself. No route lists a reference's snapshots, so the foreign attachment is not enumerable by anyone, including the reference's own registrants. ⛔ That bounds the harm and does not excuse it: an invisible write is worse evidence than a visible one, not better.
- ⭐ **DECIDED: the snapshot write takes the registration binding**, and the leaf's own warning is ANSWERED rather than obeyed. It said the asymmetry that made the snapshot replay safe — a submission carries the BYTES — cuts the other way here. It does. It is still not a reason to leave the write open, because a `SnapshotSubmission` also carries `original_locator`: a caller that can make one already holds everything registration needs, so it can register the pair, receive the SAME reference id, and file. That path is a control arm, not an assertion.
- **FIX** — the reference lookup gains the registration predicate **in the same statement**: `SELECT r.expected_digest FROM resource_references r JOIN reference_registrations g ON g.resource_id = r.resource_id AND g.tenant_id = $2 WHERE r.resource_id = $1`. ⛔ No new error variant: a reference the caller did not register is `ReferenceMissing`, the same answer an absent id gets, so there is nothing for the distinction to leak through. The message becomes *"the reference does not exist, or this tenant did not register it"* — one sentence for two cases, deliberately.
- **ADDRESSED (verified)** — the foreign reference and the absent id are refused in the SAME words and attach **0** rows; the registering tenant files normally; the second tenant registers the same locator, replays to the same reference id, files, and the submission REPLAYS to one shared snapshot row carrying **2** citations.
- ⚠️ **`.11.14.3.4`'s census stands for the routes it enumerated, and is corrected in its reach.** The correction is not to its verdicts — those hold — but to the claim a reader would take from them. Recorded in the decision record and promoted as `docs/knowledge/a-census-is-as-wide-as-its-key.md`.
- ROUTING EVIDENCE: `.11.14.3.13` is opened from this leaf's execution. `snapshots::submit` binds `submission.original_locator` straight into the insert and never compares it with the reference's — `grep -n "original_locator" crates/reasonbraid-server/src/snapshots.rs` shows the bind and no comparison — so a snapshot can record a locator its own reference does not carry. The registration binding does not close it: a registrant can still supply a different locator. It is a separate mechanism from this leaf's goal line, which is why it is its own leaf rather than folded in.
- lockstep: README.md unchanged (objective, layout and standard commands untouched; this leaf binds one HTTP write and publishes it in the book chapter that documents the evidence surfaces).
- Status: `done`.
- Verification / commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0226`.

##### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.14.3.13 — A snapshot records a locator its reference need not carry

- Opened: `pending` by `.11.14.3.11`, which bound the writer and measured that the binding does not reach this.
- 🔴 **The finding.** `SnapshotSubmission` carries `original_locator`, and `snapshots::submit` binds it straight into the `evidence_snapshots` insert. The only thing it reads from `resource_references` is the pin and the registration — never the locator. So a caller may file a snapshot that says it is an acquisition of one document while its reference names another, and §12.6's *"original reference and resolved final locator"* is then two facts that need not agree.
- ⚠️ **`final_locator` is a different field and must stay free.** A redirect legitimately ends somewhere else, which is why the receipt records both; the question is only about `original_locator`, which §12.1 calls immutable on the reference.
- ⚠️ **Not reachable through the resolvers.** All three acquisition arms build `original_locator: reference.original_locator.clone()`, so they cannot disagree by construction. The surface is `POST /v1/snapshots` alone, which is the same one `.11.14.3.11` just bound — so the caller is now a registrant of the reference, and a registrant knows its locator.
- ⛔ Do NOT assume the answer is an equality check. The column may be there to record what the ACQUISITION asked for, which can differ from the reference's spelling without being false — a case-normalised host, a trailing slash. §12.1 says canonicalization is separate and scheme-specific and must not erase security-relevant distinctions, so an equality check is a canonicalization decision wearing a different name.
- Owns: measuring what reads `evidence_snapshots.original_locator`; deciding whether it is derived from the reference, checked against it, or documented as the acquisition's own record; and stating it where the evidence contract is described.
- Acceptance: a control files a snapshot whose `original_locator` differs from its reference's and observes what is stored, RED first if the disposition is a check; the disposition is recorded with its rejected alternatives; and the book states which of the two locators a reader should trust.
- ⭐ **THE CENSUS SHAPED THE DISPOSITION, and it is the first thing the leaf asked for.** `grep -rn "original_locator" crates/reasonbraid-server/src/*.rs`: every hit outside `resources.rs` is either `reference.original_locator` — the REFERENCE's field, which the resolvers read to fetch — or the snapshot column being written, mapped into `StoredSnapshot`, and listed in the read surfaces' column set. **Nothing reads `evidence_snapshots.original_locator` to make a decision**: no resolver, no gate, no routing rule. So this is an evidence-integrity defect rather than a routing one, and a refusal is the whole repair — there is no downstream behaviour to correct, only a record that could be false.
- 🔴 **REPRODUCE, falsified against the exact unrepaired store.** A submission naming `https://example.org/some-other-document`, filed against a reference registered as `https://example.org/the-registered-report`, was **stored**: `200 {"replay":false,"snapshot_id":"snp_01a0af0ef6fe7f028d0e2014a444655b"}`; `49 passed; 1 failed`.
- ⭐ **DECIDED: byte equality with the reference's locator; `final_locator` untouched** (`docs/decisions/2026-09-17_a-snapshot-names-the-locator-its-reference-names.md`, three alternatives rejected). ⛔ **The leaf's warning is ANSWERED rather than obeyed**: *"an equality check is a canonicalization decision wearing a different name"* is true of a NORMALISING check — one that lower-cases a host or strips a trailing slash to decide two spellings are the same — and false of a STRICT one, which normalises nothing and decides nothing. §12.1's immutable locator is exactly what makes the reference's stored string the identity to compare against.
- **FIX** — the lookup `.11.14.3.11` added returns the locator alongside the pin, and a disagreement is `SnapshotError::LocatorMismatch` before anything is written. The refusal NAMES BOTH values: it runs after the registration predicate, so the caller has proved it registered the reference and may read that locator — quoting it discloses nothing it does not hold.
- **ADDRESSED (verified)** — the disagreeing submission is refused `400` naming both locators with **0** rows written; the agreeing submission is accepted **with a different `final_locator`**, and both stored values are read back and asserted. ⭐ That second arm is load-bearing: a repair that compared `final_locator` too would fail it, and would be WRONG rather than merely stricter — §12.6 records both precisely because a redirect moves one.
- ⚠️ **NO REGRESSION, and it corrected a control of my own.** `.11.14.3.6`'s pin control passed the pinned report's locator for BOTH of its references, which was simply wrong about which document the unpinned snapshot was of and which nothing checked. It now passes each reference's own locator, with every original assertion intact. ⭐ The check found a defect in this session's own test data on its first run, which is the strongest evidence it measures something real.
- lockstep: README.md unchanged (objective, layout and standard commands untouched; this leaf adds one equality check and states it in the book chapter that documents the evidence contract).
- Status: `done`.
- Verification / commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0227`.

##### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.14.3.12 — Two acquisition arms discard whether the evidence was persisted

- Opened: `pending` by `.11.14.3.6`, which gave the discard a likely cause rather than creating it.
- 🔴 **The finding.** `api.rs`'s R0 arm (`let _ = crate::snapshots::submit(…)`) and its R5 arm do exactly that, with the R0 site's own comment stating the intent: *"a persistence failure leaves the receipt returned (the acquisition succeeded)"*. Censused: `grep -n "crate::snapshots::submit" crates/reasonbraid-server/src/*.rs` returns **4** sites; the R2 arm captures its result and `submit_snapshot` matches on it, so the population is **two**.
- ⚠️ **What changed and what did not.** The discard is older than the pin. Before `.11.14.3.6` its only cause was a storage fault, which is rare and genuinely outside the caller's control. Now a pinned reference whose page has drifted takes the same path — a common, caller-meaningful outcome — and the caller receives an acquisition receipt with no snapshot behind it and nothing saying so.
- ⛔ Do NOT assume the answer is to fail the resolution. The comment's intent is defensible: the acquisition DID happen, the receipt is a true statement about the network, and turning a persistence outcome into an acquisition failure would misreport the other direction. The honest candidates are an `acquisition_error` beside the receipt, a separate `persisted` field on the outcome, or failing the request — and the third is a wire change to a shipped response.
- Owns: deciding what a resolution reports when its evidence was not persisted, and making the two arms say it.
- Acceptance: a control resolves a pinned reference whose served bytes differ and observes the silent receipt RED first; the disposition is recorded with its rejected alternatives; and the resolution's contract is stated in the book beside the pin.
- ⭐ **THE DISPOSITION WAS NOT AN OPEN QUESTION, AND THAT IS THE FINDING.** This leaf was opened naming three candidates — an `acquisition_error` beside the receipt, a `persisted` field, or failing the request. Reading the R2 arm's own call site settled it: `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.4.2` had already decided exactly this, in a comment written at the site — *"A failed snapshot is NOT a successful acquisition. This path used to discard the error and still set `outcome.acquisition`, so a caller was told the document had been acquired while no evidence row and no derivation existed."* It sets `acquisition_error { kind: "evidence_unstored" }` and returns WITHOUT an `acquisition`. ⛔ So this is a shipped decision with two unconverted call sites, not a design choice — a different and much cheaper thing to find, and it was found by MEASURING the neighbour rather than by reasoning from the leaf's own framing.
- 🔴 **REPRODUCE, falsified against the exact unconverted arms** (`git stash push -- crates/reasonbraid-server/src/api.rs`, control run, file restored). A reference pinned to bytes the origin does not serve, resolved through R0:

```json
{"acquisition":{"acquired_at":"2026-09-17T10:04:42.363813Z","byte_count":412,
  "chain":["http://127.0.0.1:56360/feed.xml","http://127.0.0.1:56360/feed.xml"],
  "content_type":"text/xml; charset=utf-8","digest":"sha256:561688a4…",
  "final_url":"http://127.0.0.1:56360/feed.xml","sniffed":"text"},
 "resolvers":["r0-https-fetcher"],"unresolvable_now":false}
```

  A complete receipt — digest, byte count, redirect chain — with **0** snapshots stored and **no** `acquisition_error` at all. `47 passed; 1 failed`.
- **FIX** — the R0 and R5 arms take the R2 shape verbatim: on `Err`, log `acquisition_evidence_unstored`, set `acquisition_error { kind: "evidence_unstored", message }`, and return without setting `acquisition`. `grep -n "let _ = crate::snapshots::submit" crates/reasonbraid-server/src/*.rs` now returns **nothing**. ⛔ No new field and no wire change: the vocabulary is the one `.7.4.2` shipped, so a client that already handles `evidence_unstored` from R2 handles it from R0 and R5 unchanged.
- **ADDRESSED (verified)** — the pinned reference's resolution answers `evidence_unstored` with NO acquisition receipt and 0 snapshots; the UNPINNED reference through the SAME deployment acquires, persists **1** snapshot and names no error — the bound that a repair reporting `evidence_unstored` for every resolution would fail. `RB_DEMO=0 bash scripts/run_pg_tests.sh profiles` → **48 passed / 0 failed**.
- ⚠️ **What this does not change**: the acquisition still HAPPENED, and the log line records it. What the caller no longer receives is a receipt implying evidence that is not there. The three candidates the leaf named are all superseded by the existing decision rather than weighed — recorded so a reader does not re-open a question `.7.4.2` closed.
- lockstep: README.md unchanged (objective, layout and standard commands untouched; this leaf converts two handler arms onto a shipped contract and states it in the book chapter that documents the pin).
- Status: `done`.
- Verification / commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0225`.

### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.12 — `rb-server` acts on its configuration before it validates it

- Opened: `pending` by `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.9.1.3.1`'s clause reconciliation of `R-36-39-9`, which no leaf had cited. Two clauses, one shape: the boot sequence commits to a decision before checking whether it is allowed to make it.
- **The finding, measured at the source.** `crates/reasonbraid-server/src/bin/rb-server.rs`:
  - `sqlx::migrate!("../../migrations").run(&pool).await?` runs on the line BEFORE `secret_store::SecretStore::resolve(&args.secret_store_profile)`, whose own comment states the contract: *"an undeclared profile refuses the boot — never a silent fallback"*. The refusal is real and it arrives after the schema has already been migrated. A typo'd profile against the wrong database leaves that database changed and no service running.
  - `host` is `#[arg(long, default_value = "127.0.0.1")]` with NO gate: `--host 0.0.0.0` binds every interface, and the startup line still prints `rb-server listening on http://{addr} (Phase 0 dev profile)`. The declared profile and the bind address are independent.
- ROUTING EVIDENCE: this is `rb-server`'s startup sequence, which no existing leaf's goal line reaches. `.9.3` owns deployment/correction/review lifecycle, `.11.3` owns the operational SCRIPTS, `.11.2` owns the doctrine gates and the bootstrap template, and `.2.1` (done) owned the repository-local execution environment. What was measured is the ORDER of two statements in `main` and the absence of any predicate on one argument; what would make the routing wrong is if the migration were idempotent-and-harmless in every deployment profile, which is a claim about profiles this project has not qualified (G6/G7 are open).
- ⚠️ **Neither half is the same defect as the other, and the leaf should not merge them.** The ordering is a fail-closed PURITY question — a refusal that has already acted. The bind gate is an exposure question whose answer may legitimately be "documented, not enforced, until the Internet profile exists". Decide them separately.
- Owns: reordering the boot so every declared-configuration refusal precedes every mutation, and DECIDING whether the bind address is gated on the declared profile or explicitly documented as ungated. ⛔ Do not silently widen the dev profile's contract in either direction.
- Acceptance: a control that boots with an undeclared profile against a database at a known migration version and proves the version UNCHANGED; and, for the bind, either a control that refuses a non-loopback bind under the dev profile or a recorded decision naming where the limit is published. ⚠️ `docs/book/src/` already carries the deployment limits the Phase-7 gate recorded — align with them rather than restating them.
- Status: `done`; REPAIR-0211.
- **THE TWO HALVES WERE DECIDED SEPARATELY, as this leaf's own text required, and they did not come out the same way.**
- **Half 1 — the ordering — is fail-closed and was never a decision.** `SecretStore::resolve` is a pure match on a string (`secret_store.rs:87`) and the address is a pure parse; neither touches the database, and both ran AFTER `sqlx::migrate!`. Both now run before `PgPool::connect`. ⭐ The comment above them says what may not follow: *nothing below this line is allowed to be a check the boot could have made first*.
- ⭐ **THE INSTRUMENT IS THE ERROR'S IDENTITY, AND IT NEEDS NO DATABASE.** Both controls point the server at `postgres://rb:rb@127.0.0.1:1/none` — a port nothing serves — so a boot that reaches the connection reports `PoolTimedOut` and a boot that refuses first reports the configuration it refused. ⛔ The acceptance asked for "a database at a known migration version"; this proves the refusal precedes the CONNECT, which is strictly EARLIER than the migration, with no PostgreSQL, no schema read-back and no port bound. ⚠️ The limit is stated in the test module's own header rather than left for a reader: it does not read a version back.
- ⭐ **The first draft of these controls was WEAKER than it read, and measuring found it.** They asserted the output did not contain `127.0.0.1:1`; under the neutralization the unrepaired boot reports `Error: PoolTimedOut`, which contains no address at all, so the bind-address control PASSED against the defect it exists to catch. Re-run against the real failure text, both now assert on `PoolTimedOut` itself. ⛔ **A control's discriminator has to be the string the failure actually prints**, not the one the author expects — and the only way to know is to run the neutralization before believing the control.
- **Half 2 — the bind — is REPORTED, NOT REFUSED, and the reason is that a gate would break a shipped capability.** `docs/book/src/deployment.md` names two supported profiles and the second is *Trusted LAN*: "The control plane binds the LAN (`rb-server --host 0.0.0.0 …`)". `deploy/`'s runbook and `scripts/demo_two_host.sh` both walk it. ⛔ And a gate would be the wrong instrument regardless: what bounds Internet exposure is G6/G7 and blockers **B1–B3** — an external threat model, a pen test, a prompt-injection suite — none of which is a property of an argument.
- ⭐ **What WAS wrong is that the startup line could not tell the two apart.** It printed `(Phase 0 dev profile)` whether the server was reachable from one loopback or from every host on the network. It now names its reach through `reasonbraid_server::bind_exposure`, a pure function with a unit control over six addresses including both IPv6 forms. The decision, its three rejected alternatives and what it deliberately does NOT claim: `docs/decisions/2026-09-16_rb-server-bind-exposure.md`.
- ⚠️ **A third defect the leaf did not name, repaired because the leaf is about refusals being useful:** `main` returns `Box<dyn Error>`, whose `Termination` prints the DEBUG form, so a typo'd `--host` reported `Error: AddrParseError(Socket)` — no argument, no value, nothing an operator could act on. It now reads ``the bind address `not a host:4310` is not a host and port``, and a control asserts that exact text.
- **FALSIFIED, self-reversing, proved restored:** moving the database work back above the two pure checks fails BOTH ordering controls — `test result: FAILED. 1 passed; 2 failed` — while `a_declared_profile_still_reaches_the_database` stays green, which is the matched pair: a repair that refused every boot would fail that one instead. Restoring and `cmp -s` reports byte-identical; the positive control afterwards is 3 passed / 0 failed.
- Verification: `python3 -B scripts/project_env.py cargo test -p reasonbraid-server --test server_boot --locked` rc=0, **3 passed / 0 failed**; `cargo test -p reasonbraid-server --lib --locked` rc=0, **112 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored** (the new `bind_exposure` control is the 112th). `cargo clippy -p reasonbraid-server --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` rc=0; `cargo fmt --all -- --check` rc=0; `make gate` rc=0; `mdbook build docs/book` and `scripts/check_book_links.sh` rc=0.
- promotion: declined (the transferable half — a control's discriminator must be the string the failure actually prints — is an instance of `neutralize-into-the-fix-you-almost-wrote`'s own rule that the neutralization is what tells you whether the control works, and it is recorded at this leaf where the next reader of these controls will meet it).
- Commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0211 (leaf SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.12): every configuration refusal happens before the first mutation`.

### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.11 — An `attach` row's next action is the one thing the ledger cannot check

- Opened: `pending` by the director's grading question on 2026-09-14, which sent this session back over its own published claims (`docs/CLAIM_VERIFICATION.md`: being asked "do you still stand by it?" IS the grading event).

- **census, run before proposing the rule** (`.11.6`'s standing requirement): **15** `attach` rows today across seven owner leaves (`.4.1`, `.5.1`, `.7.1` ×3, `.8.1`, `.9.2`, `.10.2` ×2, `.11.4`). Checking each owner's own section for its record id inside an `ATTACHED CLAUSE` block: **15 of 15 present, 0 breaching**. At tranche 1's close the same check would have reported **3 breaching of 3**.
- ⭐ **That is the `REASON-CODE-DOC` shape and NOT `.11.9`'s rejected shape**, and the distinction is the whole reason this is worth proposing: it fires on **0** today, would have fired on every historical instance, and its population is bounded by a single tracked file. `.11.9`'s rejected gate would have fired on 114 of 131 on the day it was registered.
- Owns: extending `scripts/census_record_reconciliation.py --classified` with one more refusal — an `attach` row whose owner leaf's own section does not name its record — plus the self-test controls that fire it, and a `DOCTRINE_ENFORCEMENT.md` line if it is registered.
- ⚠️ **The rule must be stated over the OWNER's section, not over a phrase.** Matching prose would have to guess at paraphrase, which is the failure mode `.11.6` measures; the sound rule is the one already run by hand: the record id appears in the owning leaf's own section. ⛔ Do NOT require the literal string `ATTACHED CLAUSE` — that is this session's formatting convention, not a contract.
- ⚠️ Reproduce the historical 3-of-3 at tranche 1's commit before registering, so the "would have fired" claim is measured rather than reasoned.
- Acceptance: the census is reproduced at both points, the refusal is added with a control that has been observed RED, `--classified` stays clean on the current ledger, and the gate is either registered or explicitly declined with its reason.
- Status: `done`; REPAIR-0176. **Registered as `ATTACH-LANDED`.**

⭐ **The census was reproduced at FOUR points rather than the two the acceptance asked for, and by TWO independent routes.** The leaf's "would have fired" claim was written before any instrument could test it, so it was tested the only way that settles it: a detached worktree at each tranche's closing commit, with the NEW instrument copied in and run against the OLD ledger and the OLD trees.

| Commit | Tranche closed | `attach` rows | breaching | rc |

The question it did not ask is the one that mattered: **if all 26 are durable elsewhere, why is any of them in the pointer at all?** The data supported this repair eleven commits before it happened. ⚠️ A census answers the question it was given; the framing is the part to falsify.

#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.4.2.3 — The rewritten pointer did not follow the specification that governs it

- Opened: `pending` by the director, 2026-09-16: *"MEMORY.md is governed by the memory architecture document so please stick to the defined rules."*
- 🔴 **The defect, stated plainly: DOC-0032 rewrote layer A from the director's one-line instruction and `COMMIT.md`, and did not re-read `MEMORY_ARCHITECTURE.md` §6 — which specifies the file's exact template.** ⛔ `CLAUDE.md` lists that document as **MANDATORY** reading and §6 ends with a fenced block introduced as *"the entire contents of a demoted `MEMORY.md`"*. The rewrite was an improvement over a 7,168-byte log and was still an invented structure where a specified one existed.
- **The five deviations, enumerated rather than summarised:**
  1. The title dropped the template's own cap reminder — `(layer A; overwrite-only, keep ≤ ~50 lines)`.
  2. `## How to resume` did not name `MEMORY_ARCHITECTURE.md`, which is the template's FIRST line and the one that routes a fresh agent to the system of record.
  3. 🔴 **The `Current state` block used free-form bullets instead of the five named fields, and OMITTED `in_flight_uncommitted` entirely.** That is the costly one: it is the field that tells a resuming session whether work is stranded, and it is exactly what `MEMORY_ARCHITECTURE.md` §3 says layer A holds — *"any in-flight uncommitted work"*.
  4. The block heading dropped `(OVERWRITE this block each update — do not append)`. The rule was stated once at the top of the file instead of on the block it governs, which is where the next author is looking.
  5. Three sections the template does not have — `Standing obligations`, `Traps`, `Where the rest lives`.
- ⛔ **And deviation 5 was a layer violation, not just a shape one.** The "traps" were `python3 -B scripts/project_env.py cargo …` and one-cargo-at-a-time — **environment quirks**, which §4's write path assigns to layer C by name: *"an environment quirk … → write a decision record (C)"*. They were already there: `docs/decisions/2026-09-09_repository-local-command-environment.md` carries `project_env.py` at lines 21 and 63–70. ⭐ So the rewrite that removed a log of durable facts from the pointer put two more durable facts back into it, in the same commit.
- **The measurement, three points:** the file was **26 lines / 7,168 bytes** (a log), became **35 / 3,583** (invented structure), and is now **16 lines / 1,395 bytes** — 34 lines and 5,773 bytes free — carrying the template's five fields. ⛔ No cap was raised at any point.
- ⭐ **What DOC-0032 got right is not withdrawn**: the partition was correct, the 14 leavers are durable, and the census still reports 0 standing warnings. What it got wrong is that it derived the target shape from a conversation instead of from the file that defines it — and `MEMORY_ARCHITECTURE.md` §1 names an "ever-growing `MEMORY.md`" as the exact failure mode, so the specification had already thought about this harder than the rewrite did.
- ⚠️ **Routed, not absorbed:** §6 says *"Prefer derived over hand-written — a small script can regenerate the current-state block … so it cannot drift."* Four of the five fields are mechanically derivable and one is a judgement sentence. That is the opposite ratio to `.11.4.5.3`, which REJECTED its generator on a census finding 13 of 14 rows were curated prose — so the precedent does not transfer, and the census is still owed before anything is proposed (`.11.6`). New owner `.11.4.2.4`.
- Acceptance: `MEMORY.md` carries the §6 template's section headings and its five named fields, `in_flight_uncommitted` included; every deviation is enumerated with what it cost; the environment quirks are shown to be already recorded in layer C rather than merely deleted; the size is stated against both caps with headroom; and the derived-pointer question is routed with its census owed rather than answered.
- Status: `done`; DOC-0033.
- Verification: `bash scripts/check_memory_architecture.sh` rc=0 with `wc -l` **16 of 50** and `wc -c` **1395 of 7168**. `grep -n "project_env" docs/decisions/2026-09-09_repository-local-command-environment.md` returns lines 21, 63, 64, 65 and 70, which is the evidence that deviation 5 deleted nothing durable. `python3 -B scripts/census_memory_warnings.py` reports `MEMORY.md standing warnings: 0`.
- promotion: declined (the transferable half — read the specification that governs an artefact before rewriting it — is `CLAUDE.md`'s mandatory-reading rule and `docs/CLAIM_VERIFICATION.md`'s "verify the premise the decision turns on" met from a third angle; this is an instance, recorded here, not a new statement).

#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.4.2.4 — Whether the resume pointer's current-state block should be derived

- Opened: `pending` by `.11.4.2.3`, routing §6's preference rather than acting on it.
- The requirement, verbatim from `MEMORY_ARCHITECTURE.md` §6: *"**Prefer derived over hand-written** — a small script can regenerate the current-state block from `git log` + each tree's frontier row, so it cannot drift."* Today every field is hand-written.
- **What is derivable, field by field**, from the §6 template's five: `latest_commit` and the ahead-count from `git log -1` and `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD`; `active_work_unit` and the frontier leaf with its status from the tree's Current Frontier row 1, which `scripts/check_tree_index_frontier.sh` already parses; `in_flight_uncommitted` from `git status --porcelain`. **Four of five.** `next_action` is a judgement sentence and must be preserved, never generated.
- ⛔ **`.11.4.5.3` REJECTED its generator and the precedent does NOT transfer — say why rather than citing it.** There the census found regenerating the tree index's column *"would destroy accurate curated prose in 13 of 14 rows"*. Here the ratio is inverted: four of five fields are mechanical and the one curated field is a single line a generator can leave untouched. ⚠️ That is an argument for measuring, not a licence to skip it.
- census owed before anything is proposed (`.11.6`, and `.11.4.5.3`'s own reversal): how often each derivable field has been WRONG in `MEMORY.md`'s history — `git log -p -- MEMORY.md` against the commit each version was written at. ⭐ A generator is worth building if the fields drift and worth declining if they do not, and this session already carried a stale `133 commits ahead` for ten commits and incremented it twice without re-deriving, so the expected answer is not zero.
- ⚠️ A generator that rewrites this file can destroy `next_action`. Whatever is built preserves that line unless explicitly given a new one, and a control must observe it surviving a regeneration.
- Acceptance: the drift census is run and recorded with its command; the decision to generate or decline is taken ON that measurement and recorded either way; if generated, the instrument is tracked with a `--self-test`, a control proves `next_action` survives, and the currency check is registered or explicitly declined with its reason.

###### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.4.3.1.7.1 — The cluster instrument's self-test could only ever pass once

- Opened: `pending`; found on 2026-09-13 by RUNNING `--self-test` before acting on the instrument's census, which is the only reason it was noticed.
- 🔴 The finding: `census_pg_test_clusters.py --self-test` exits 1 with `SELF-TEST FAILED: citation guard: an absent name reported references`. The guard's absent-name arm searches tracked files for the literal `run-selftest-no-such-cluster-name` and asserts zero hits — but **that literal is written in the instrument's own source**, which is a tracked file, so `git grep -c -- "run-selftest-no-such-cluster-name"` returns `scripts/census_pg_test_clusters.py:1`. The control searches for a string it contains.
- **Dated rather than estimated:** `git log --diff-filter=A -- scripts/census_pg_test_clusters.py` and `git log -S "run-selftest-no-such-cluster-name"` both name the SAME commit, `cb2f197` (REPAIR-0107, leaf `.11.4.3.1.7`). So the arm passed exactly once — while the file was still untracked and `git grep` could not see it — and has failed from the instant it was committed.
- census of why that survived, the claim one counterexample would refute: `git grep -n "census_pg_test_clusters" -- scripts .githooks .github Makefile knowledge-map` returns **2** hits and both are inside the instrument's own usage docstring. **Nothing invokes it**, self-test or otherwise. Widened to the enforcer: `grep -n "self-test" scripts/check_doctrines.sh` returns **0** — the registered doctrine checks carry `--self-test` arms too, and the enforcer runs none of them. Author-run only, across the board.
- ⚠️ What this does and does not compromise, stated precisely because the instrument guards a deletion: the guard's OTHER direction (a tracked filename reports non-zero) still passes, so cited clusters were still protected. What was lost is the proof that the guard is not simply returning non-zero for everything — i.e. the guard was half-verified, and a half-verified safety check must not authorise retiring 1.8 GB.
- Owns: making the probe a name that CANNOT appear in a tracked file (generated per run rather than written as a literal), so the control cannot poison itself again; and deciding whether the instrument's self-test gains a runner, since "nothing ran it" is the reason a control could sit broken from its own first commit.
- ⛔ Do not simply exclude the script from the grep: that would make the guard blind to the one file most likely to name a cluster in a comment, and it treats the symptom rather than the self-reference.
- Acceptance: `--self-test` exits 0 with both citation directions firing; the absent-name probe is demonstrably absent by construction, not by luck; the §8 retirement runs only after the instrument's own control passes.
- Status: `done`; REPAIR-0137.
- Fix: the absent-name probe is `f"run-selftest-{uuid.uuid4().hex}"`, generated per run. A literal written in a tracked file can never be absent from the tracked tree; a fresh uuid always is. The comment beside it names the trap so the next author does not re-introduce a literal, and the failure message now prints the probe it used, so a future failure says WHICH name was found rather than restating a constant.
- ⛔ The `git grep` was deliberately NOT narrowed to exclude this script, per the leaf's own prohibition: that would blind the guard to the one file most likely to name a cluster in a comment, and it treats the symptom rather than the self-reference.

###### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.4.3.1.7.2 — Nothing runs a `--self-test`

- Opened: `pending` by `.11.4.3.1.7.1`, whose repaired control had been failing from its own first commit because no runner existed to notice.
- census, recorded here rather than in the parent because the claim quantifies over the tree: `git grep -n "census_pg_test_clusters" -- scripts .githooks .github Makefile knowledge-map` returns **2** hits, both inside the instrument's own usage docstring — nothing invokes it. Widened to the enforcer that would be the natural runner, `grep -n "self-test" scripts/check_doctrines.sh` returns **0**, so none of the 17 registered doctrine checks has its `--self-test` arm run either. Author-run only, across the board.
- Owns: deciding whether self-tests get a runner, and which. ⛔ Census owed first, per `.11.6`: how many tracked scripts HAVE a `--self-test`, how long each takes, and whether running them in the pre-commit enforcer is affordable against the gate's existing cost — `make gate` is on every commit, and a gate people route around is a gate that lies (`.11.5`'s binding constraint).
- ⚠️ Widened on 2026-09-13 by `.3.5`'s census, which ran every census instrument's `--self-test` before trusting its output (this leaf's own lesson, applied): `census_admission_paths.py` reports 5/5 and `census_pg_test_clusters.py` passes, but **`census_authority_paths.py` has no `--self-test` at all** — it takes the flag as a git revision and dies with a `CalledProcessError` traceback rather than a usage error. So the population is not only "self-tests nothing runs" but also "instruments with no self-test to run", and this leaf owns counting both.
- ⚠️ The obvious rule — "the enforcer runs every self-test" — may be wrong in the way `.11.4.5.3`'s generator was. Some self-tests spawn processes or touch the filesystem, and a pre-commit hook is not the place for all of them. Measure before proposing.
- Acceptance: the census is recorded with its command; the decision names which self-tests run where, with the cost measured rather than assumed; "measured and deliberately not mechanized" stays a legitimate outcome.
- Status: `done`; REPAIR-0142. Mechanized, and the cost was measured before the rule was proposed rather than after.
- **The census, with its commands.** `git grep -l -- "--self-test" -- scripts knowledge-map .githooks | wc -l` -> **17** scripts carry one; `ls scripts/check_*.sh knowledge-map/scripts/check_*.sh scripts/census_*.py | wc -l` -> **28** check/census scripts in total. So **11 have no `--self-test` at all**, which the widened finding at `.3.5` had already shown for `census_authority_paths.py`.
- **The cost, measured rather than estimated, because `.11.5`'s constraint is binding.** Running all 17 takes **1.01 s** in total (the slowest is `census_pg_test_clusters.py` at 0.23 s; twelve are under 0.05 s), and `make gate` costs **3.15 s**. With the new check registered the gate measures **4.27 s** over 18 checks — a real increase of 1.12 s. One second on a three-second gate is not a gate anyone routes around, which is exactly the test `.11.5` set.
- **The decision: MECHANIZE.** `scripts/check_self_tests.sh`, registered as `SELF-TEST` and mirrored in `DOCTRINE_ENFORCEMENT.md`. It DISCOVERS the population rather than carrying a list, so a new instrument with a self-test is covered the day it lands — which is the property a hand-maintained list would lose the first time someone forgot.
- ⛔ **The gate catches NOTHING today and the check says so in its own header.** All 17 pass. Its value is preventing the `.11.4.3.1.7.1` class — a control that silently stops working — not finding a present defect. A green run is not evidence of one.
- 🔴 **I fell into this gate's own trap while building it, and the defence is stronger because of it.** The check warns at length about self-reference, and excluding its own path was the obvious guard. It was not enough: REGISTERING the check put the flag's literal text into `check_doctrines.sh`'s description, so discovery found the **ENFORCER**, ran it with the flag, and the enforcer — which ignores unknown arguments — ran every check including this one. Unbounded recursion on the first `make gate` after registration; the command was killed at 400 s. The gate exists because a control searched for a string it contained, and building it I made a discovery match a string it had just written.
- Defended twice now, the first making the failure impossible rather than unlikely: an exported `RB_SELF_TEST_GATE` makes any nested invocation exit immediately, so no discovery mistake can recurse; and the enforcer is excluded by path because it is the RUNNER, not a check. Both are asserted by the self-test, alongside the failing-arm and passing-arm directions.
- ⚠️ Residual, in the script's header rather than hidden: a script that merely MENTIONS the flag without implementing it is run with an argument it ignores — i.e. run normally. Every member of the discovered population is a read-only check or census, so that is harmless today; it would not be for a mutating script, and a future one must be excluded there.
- Verification: `bash scripts/check_self_tests.sh --self-test` prints `a failing arm caught, a passing one ignored, neither this script nor the enforcer discovered, the recursion guard short-circuits, 17 scripts discovered`, rc=0 — four-sided. `bash scripts/check_self_tests.sh` rc=0 in 1.05 s. `make gate` prints `=== all doctrines green ===` across **18 checks** in 4.27 s. `mdbook build` and `bash scripts/check_book_links.sh` rc=0, `git diff --check` rc=0.
- **FALSIFIED end to end against the real defect, not a synthetic one**: restoring `census_pg_test_clusters.py`'s literal probe — the exact `.11.4.3.1.7.1` defect — makes `make gate` print `❌ SELF-TEST`, quote `citation guard: the absent name run-selftest-no-such-cluster-name reported references`, and refuse the commit with `1 doctrine breach(es)`. Restoring the repair returns it to green. The gate would have caught the defect that motivated it, on the commit that introduced it.
- ⛔ NOT claimed: this does not give the 11 script without a self-test one, and does not assert that the 17 self-tests are GOOD — only that they still pass. A weak self-test that passes is invisible to this gate, as it should be: judging a control's strength is a reader's job, and `.11.5`'s accepted item (1) — a control must have failed on the defect it was written for — is the separate rule for that.
- promotion: declined for a new `docs/knowledge/` record — the durable statement is the registered doctrine itself, whose `DOCTRINE_ENFORCEMENT.md` row carries the measurement, the cost, what it does not catch, and the recursion it fell into. That is the strongest form this project has.
- Commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0142 (leaf SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.4.3.1.7.2): run the self-tests, including the one this gate fell into`.
